0b33ce1ee1a26d14.title: For Critical Minerals, Money Isn’t the Problem. Commitment Is.
0b33ce1ee1a26d14.summary: The money is finally flowing. What Washington lacks is a constituency that won’t let the next Congress walk away.

ai.sum: Commentary argues Washington's critical minerals funding is flowing but lacks durable political commitment to sustain it across Congresses.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Washington's problem with critical minerals is not a shortage of money but a commitment problem: a future Congress can abandon a decade-long supply-chain build-out. Government funds are flowing through the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital, yet private investors find rare-earth projects unprofitable. To lock in durable support, they propose three mechanisms: creating a group purchasing organization to pool demand and set prices, trading guaranteed offtake for coinvestment by strategic buyers, and tracking a portfolio-level scorecard of wins and losses. They also suggest built-in sunsets tied to performance. The aim is to turn defense contractors, automakers and chipmakers into a constituency that defends the program across administrations.
brief.argument: Durable US critical-minerals supply requires building a domestic constituency with its own financial stake, since funding alone cannot survive shifting political cycles.
recommendations: Create a group purchasing organization to aggregate demand and enable price discovery, using Defense Production Act Section 708 voluntary agreements
Reserve a share of offtake for vetted strategic coinvestors who invest pro rata alongside the government
Track wins and losses across the whole of government in a portfolio scorecard to defend the program against Solyndra-style backlash
Attach built-in sunsets to subsidies tied to output and performance targets rather than fixed end dates

75bcf63463a331bc.title: Congress could soon rein in Trump’s tariffs on Canada. Here’s what that could look like.
75bcf63463a331bc.summary: Removing Section 338 tariffs on Canada may be a good place to start for the new Congress. The post Congress could soon rein in Trump’s tariffs on Canada. Here’s what that could look like. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council piece suggests Congress could move to curb Trump's Section 338 tariffs on Canada.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Congress may soon repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the authority Trump used in August to impose 50 percent tariffs on roughly twenty billion dollars of Canadian goods, with enough bipartisan support to override a veto. They estimate that repeal would pull the average US tariff rate on Canadian goods back to about 3 percent and lower costs for importers, while Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US exports could ease. However, they stress that Section 301 and Section 232 tariffs, the USMCA non-renewal and the looming auto tariff increase would persist, so repeal would relieve some tension but not resolve the broader relationship. They describe Section 338 as a relatively low-cost first step, since it sits apart from the wider tariff regime and its use requires no process or investigation.
brief.argument: Repealing Section 338 tariffs on Canada would ease trade tensions quickly, but the broader US-Canada tariff and trust problems would remain.
recommendations: Congress should repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and be prepared to override a presidential veto
Congress should provide timely refunds for tariffs already paid under Section 338
Washington and Ottawa should negotiate a deal to avoid the scheduled doubling of auto and parts tariffs in January 2027

brief.summary: The authors, WHO leaders and public health specialists, argue that cervical cancer could become the first cancer ever eliminated, using existing tools of HPV vaccination, screening and timely treatment. They stress the disease's stark inequality, with 19 of the 20 highest-burden countries in WHO's African Region, and frame elimination as a story of science, solidarity and sustained commitment. They point to the 2020 WHO Global Strategy targets of 90% HPV vaccination for girls, 70% screening coverage and 90% access to treatment. They cite progress: Australia and Sweden nearing elimination, Rwanda's districts meeting targets, 166 countries with HPV vaccination in national programmes, and vaccine supply constraints largely overcome. The piece is an advocacy article rather than an analysis of obstacles or costs.
brief.argument: Cervical cancer can be eliminated as a public health problem using existing HPV vaccination, screening and treatment tools, and accelerating progress shows this is achievable.
recommendations: Meet the WHO targets of 90% HPV vaccination coverage for girls, 70% screening coverage for women and 90% access to treatment for precancerous lesions or cancer

brief.summary: The authors argue that China's AI market correction, with the STAR 50 losing about 40% in under four months, does not prove AI is a bubble, but exposes doubts about spending, utilisation and revenue. They contrast China's reported rack occupancy of 71.4% with estimated computing utilisation of roughly 30-37%, describing a mismatch of idle or misplaced capacity alongside shortages of advanced chips. Globally, they note capex is rising toward $700bn-$1tn while direct AI revenue lags the roughly $500bn-$650bn annual return needed to justify infrastructure. They point to further bottlenecks: Nvidia's leadership crisis and stranded H200 inventory, Anthropic's large computing commitments, Microsoft's data-centre delays, and an outage with concentrated cloud risk. Productivity gains are real but concentrated in narrow tasks, so aggregate returns remain uncertain.
brief.argument: China's AI sell-off signals a widening gap between AI infrastructure spending and realised returns, though demand and real productivity gains persist.

130624c3ea60510f.title: El Salvador’s Troops Are Fighting Haiti’s Gangs. Who Is Protecting Civilians?
130624c3ea60510f.summary: El Salvador’s troop surge has given Haitians hope, but it has also added another armed force to an already uncoordinated fight. Four steps could protect civilians and expand aid access as military operations intensify.

brief.summary: The authors argue that El Salvador's troop surge into Haiti has raised hope among Haitians but added another uncoordinated armed force to an already fragmented security effort. Drawing on incidents such as friendly-fire close calls, a U.S. diplomatic protest, and President Bukele's crowdsourced targeting on X, they warn that the military escalation lacks civilian protection and deconfliction. They point to worsening humanitarian indicators, including record hunger and displacement, and to Vectus Global's drone strikes that have killed civilians. They contend that military action without a strategic plan to hold territory and meet humanitarian needs will likely worsen conditions. The piece frames Haiti's government and partners as facing a choice between unified operations that protect civilians and fragmented armed actors pursuing separate aims.
brief.argument: Escalating militarised operations against Haiti's gangs, without coordination, civilian protection and a plan to hold and rebuild territory, will worsen the humanitarian crisis.
recommendations: Include the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs in the Haitian government's new security coordination cell.
Require Salvadoran troops to undergo the same civilian-protection training as the GSF.
Convene an international donor conference focused on shelter and health care, and set up an international monitoring mechanism covering Salvadoran operations.
Hold an open UN Security Council meeting on Haiti and publicly release the El Salvador force agreement and rules of engagement.

a4e62d2905c4f138.title: China and Nuclear Arms Control: Why a Trump-Xi Breakthrough at APEC Is Unlikely
a4e62d2905c4f138.summary: China has historical and strategic reasons for its reluctance to engage on arms control. There are still areas that the U.S. should pursue.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a Trump-Xi-Putin nuclear breakthrough at APEC is unlikely, because China's reluctance to join arms control rests on deep historical and strategic beliefs. They trace this to a view that arms control constrains weaker states, to a deterrent that relies on uncertainty about warhead numbers and locations, to status concerns tied to Xi's leadership, and to the goal of deterring U.S. nuclear options in a Taiwan conflict. They note China is not opposed in principle, but its conditions, such as no-first-use and an end to missile defence, clash with current U.S. policy. The authors suggest Washington focus on narrower, mutually useful areas, such as missile launch notifications and tactical nuclear deployments, and keep channels open to reduce misperception in a crisis.
brief.argument: China's entrenched strategic and historical reasons make a near-term trilateral nuclear breakthrough unlikely, so the U.S. should pursue narrower, mutually beneficial arms control measures.
recommendations: Focus talks on areas of mutual concern that do not touch core national priorities
Pursue ballistic missile launch notifications that meet international norms
Explore limits on tactical nuclear weapons deployments
Establish regular bilateral channels on nuclear policy and strategic views to curb unintended escalation

d8f05d7728347c55.summary: In August 2026, the Cambodian government announced it had eliminated the country’s notorious online scam centres. Crisis Group visited Sihanoukville, where the industry took root, and found that while the declaration is largely accurate, the industry for criminal services is intact.

brief.summary: The authors visited Sihanoukville, the Cambodian city where online scam centres took root, to test the government's August 2026 claim that the centres had been eliminated. They find the declaration largely accurate in the sense that the large compounds themselves are empty, but argue that the wider industry supplying criminal services has not disappeared. Their reporting suggests the operations have dispersed and reorganised rather than been dismantled, leaving the underlying networks, labour flows and service providers intact. The piece treats official success claims with scepticism and frames the issue as one of displacement rather than eradication.
brief.argument: Cambodia has emptied its scam compounds, but the criminal services industry behind them remains intact and has likely dispersed.

86331fdc90486965.title: Spain votes first: What its snap election could mean for Europe and the United States
86331fdc90486965.summary: With nationalist parties gaining ground across Europe, Sánchez’s record offers a warning about the limits of mobilizing voters against them. The post Spain votes first: What its snap election could mean for Europe and the United States appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that Spain's snap election on 29 November is a bellwether for the European electoral cycle, with the centre-right Partido Popular and the nationalist Vox likely to win a majority. They attribute Vox's rise less to economic weakness than to housing and rail-safety failures, eroded accountability around corruption cases, and Sánchez's reliance on decree-laws and polarising rhetoric, which they say feeds the distrust populists exploit. They contend that Sánchez's record shows containing nationalists by mobilising against them can backfire. On foreign policy, they argue his NATO resistance, the Ceuta crisis and enlargement bargaining weakened Spain's European standing, and that a new government would face choices on NATO spending, Chinese investment such as SAIC's Ferrol plant and Huawei contracts, and Latin America, including Venezuela.
brief.argument: Sánchez's pursuit of political survival, polarisation and weak accountability have fed the nationalist right that his government sought to contain, and his foreign policy has cost Spain influence in Europe.
recommendations: Governments should address the discontent behind nationalist appeal, such as housing and public services, rather than portraying nationalists as the threat.
Demonstrate accountability through a government's own conduct, including respect for independent scrutiny and judicial processes.
Spain should meet NATO's spending target with sustained funding and procurement planning.
Spain should push Latin America higher on the EU agenda and support initiatives such as Global Gateway.

brief.summary: The author argues that Lagos is a genuine battleground in Nigeria's January presidential election, not a state Tinubu quietly conceded in 2023. He rejects the theory that the Tinubu campaign gave Lagos away, pointing to the state's centrality to Tinubu's political career and to real mobilisation for Peter Obi among Igbo residents, Lagosian elites and the urban precariat. He then argues that the contest is shaped by a deeper, long-running dispute over 'ownership' of Lagos between Yoruba and Igbo communities, framed as a question of identity, citizenship and belonging. He illustrates this with the Oba of Lagos's 2015 threat to Igbo traditional rulers, and notes that such indigene-versus-settler contention dates back to the colonial press. His view is that the election will be shaped by this undercurrent, with low-level rancour and possible sporadic violence on polling day.
brief.argument: Lagos will be a fiercely contested battleground because the struggle over who 'owns' the city, rooted in Yoruba-Igbo contention over identity and belonging, runs deeper than the personal rivalry between Obi and Tinubu.

0f912f8fd96924aa.summary: Ukraine hit and partially destroyed the Crimean Bridge on November 17 with an unprecedented drone and missile strike that highlighted Russia's vulnerabilities and served as a very personal humiliation for Vladimir Putin, writes Peter Dickinson. The post Ukraine’s Crimean Bridge attack is a very personal humiliation for Putin appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Analysis argues Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge was a very personal humiliation for Vladimir Putin, exposing Russian vulnerabilities.

brief.summary: The author argues that Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which destroyed its central road section and main arch, has significant military and symbolic consequences. Militarily, the road span's loss complicates resupply of occupied Crimea and Russian forces in southern Ukraine, pushing traffic onto a land route under Ukrainian drone fire. The piece also presents the attack as evidence of Ukraine's growing long-range strike capability and as a sign that Russian layered air defences around key infrastructure can be penetrated. Symbolically, the author treats the bridge as central to Putin's personal image and says the timing, just before a trilateral meeting with US and Chinese leaders, makes the blow especially humiliating. Reconstruction is expected to wait for a peace deal.
brief.argument: The Crimean Bridge strike has serious logistical effects on Russia's occupation and southern front, but its greatest impact is the personal humiliation it inflicts on Putin.

ec2c54242e2c1dd0.title: Positive economic statecraft in a fractured world: Development finance and cooperation as geoeconomic instruments—ASEAN in focus
ec2c54242e2c1dd0.summary: Positive economic statecraft (PES) was conceptualized in a macro and geoeconomic landscape that has changed considerably. Official development assistance fell 23 percent in 2025 alone, the steepest decline on record. Southeast Asia offers a particularly instructive lens on what PES looks like under these conditions, illuminating both the potential and the limits of PES as a development cooperation approach. The post Positive economic statecraft in a fractured world:…

brief.summary: The authors argue that positive economic statecraft (PES), the use of grants, concessional finance, preferential trade and guarantees to shape government behaviour, needs rethinking as aid contracts and the development finance field fragments. They use ASEAN as a lens: it is both a target of Western economic statecraft and a practitioner of its own. They describe a credibility gap, where Western donors pledge at scale but deliver less, more slowly and on harder terms while still asking for policy commitments. They note that China's lending has shifted from infrastructure toward energy and minerals, and that multilateral banks are reforming tools to deliver policy-linked concessional finance faster. Recipients now hold more leverage in a buyer's market, and ASEAN governments increasingly run several offers at once, with some setting their own standards-alignment and market-access conditions. Just Energy Transition Partnerships are cited as an example of ask-offer disparity.
brief.argument: Positive economic statecraft can still help development cooperation, but only if Western donors close a credibility gap in delivery and coherence while recipients in a multipolar market use competing offers to set the terms.
recommendations: Make inducements proportionate, timely and additional, so offers are credible against alternatives
Coordinate the competing development finance institutions so that the overall offer is coherent
Design partnerships such as JETPs with host consultation and a larger grant share
Treat blended finance as PES only when the concessional tranche is tied to a sovereign policy commitment

9dfaa914ddb70a17.title: As the Nvidia scandal threatens to reignite trade tensions at Trump-Xi talks, Beijing still holds the rare earths
9dfaa914ddb70a17.summary: Washington’s push to close loopholes could invite renewed Chinese restrictions on rare earths, exposing a supply-chain vulnerability that the trade truce never resolved. The post As the Nvidia scandal threatens to reignite trade tensions at Trump-Xi talks, Beijing still holds the rare earths appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Nvidia-Megaspeed chip-diversion scandal, alongside the espionage allegations around a former Megaspeed executive, is pushing Congress and Commerce toward tighter semiconductor export controls just as Trump and Xi prepare to meet. They contend that any such US tightening could prompt Beijing to retaliate by reinstating suspended rare earth restrictions, including its October 2025 rules on refining equipment and foreign products containing Chinese-origin rare earths. The piece stresses that China's April 2025 licensing regime still limits shipments even after licenses are approved, and that US alternative mining and refining projects are years from production. It concludes that export controls, rather than tariffs, could become the main point of contention in 2027, and that Washington would benefit from a coordinated allied response to China's licensing and nonmarket practices.
brief.argument: Tighter US chip export controls could trigger Chinese rare earth retaliation that the US is not yet equipped to absorb, making export controls the central trade flashpoint for 2027.
recommendations: Pass bipartisan export control legislation, such as the chip-location verification and allied equipment-alignment measures, in the year-end defence bill
Coordinate a joint allied response to China's rare earth licensing regime and broader nonmarket practices
Invest in long-term diversification of critical mineral supply and refining capacity

5e096008125348ee.title: What Trump, Putin, and Xi want from their meeting in Shenzhen
5e096008125348ee.summary: Atlantic Council experts answer seven pressing questions ahead of the meeting of the US, Russia, and Chinese presidents. The post What Trump, Putin, and Xi want from their meeting in Shenzhen appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts set out what Trump, Putin and Xi want from their meeting in Shenzhen.

brief.summary: The authors, a panel of Atlantic Council experts, examine the proposed Shenzhen trilateral between Trump, Putin and Xi, and what each leader and the affected parties want from it. They argue Putin sees the meeting as a Yalta-style arrangement that could press Ukraine and reads recent US concessions as enabling Moscow's war. Xi seeks to show convening power ahead of the Party Congress while avoiding surprises. Trump is expected to prioritise optics and precedent over concrete deliverables, with Iran, arms control and Ukraine on the agenda. The experts expect little substantive nuclear progress, since China rejects trilateral talks and Russia links participation to Western nuclear arsenals. Ukrainians and Europeans view the format with alarm at great-power dealmaking over smaller states, while East Asian allies worry about abandonment or entrapment.
brief.argument: The trilateral is primarily a show of great-power convening, with substantive outcomes unlikely and each participant pursuing its own interests, to the unease of Ukraine, Europe and Indo-Pacific allies.
recommendations: Allies should hold follow-on consultations with Indo-Pacific partners to ensure strategic coherence and reassure them of US collective-defence commitments.
Any request for Chinese help on Ukraine should be made in a group setting including Europeans, so they share the price China may ask.
Trilateral precedent on arms control and Iran could ease future talks, even without immediate agreement.

brief.summary: The authors interview Joel Wuthnow, who revisits his 2025 argument that Beijing's most attractive option in a Taiwan war may be to keep the United States out of the fight by threatening the American homeland rather than striking U.S. forces first. Wuthnow assesses developments since then, pointing to Pentagon reporting on the DF-27 missile, a possible move toward launch-on-warning nuclear posture, and expanded silo fields. He reads displays at the September 2025 Beijing parade, including the JL-3 and DF-61, as a new triad aimed at Washington, and cites a July 2026 submarine-launched missile test and joint bomber patrols with Russia as further signalling. He argues these capabilities could allow nuclear signalling in a crisis and raise the risk of inadvertent escalation if Washington intervenes. The excerpt is cut off before the full assessment is given.
brief.argument: China's strengthening of long-range and nuclear strategic capabilities aimed at the U.S. homeland is designed to deter Washington from intervening over Taiwan.

brief.summary: The piece, published by Al Majalla, argues that Robert Pattinson enters the role of James Bond from a position of strength, since he is already a global star. It traces how earlier Bond actors such as Sean Connery, Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig were largely made famous by the franchise, whereas Pattinson's fame predates it. The authors then walk through ten films, from Cosmopolis to Prime Time, that they present as shaping his range. They stress his shift from the Twilight franchise towards demanding roles with directors such as Cronenberg, Denis, Eggers, Nolan and Bong Joon Ho, and his willingness to play marginalised or unlikeable characters.
brief.argument: Pattinson's varied filmography, built with world-class directors, gives him an established star identity that combines with the Bond character when he takes over the role.

brief.argument: Trump's domestic weakness will drive him to seek pomp and calm-preserving diplomacy in Asia rather than substantive breakthroughs.

1e35ab65e5d9ab03.title: Ukraine Straddles Diverging Fronts
1e35ab65e5d9ab03.summary: Ukraine’s battlefield prospects are improving while Russian forces deteriorate, but damage is accumulating in the rear and funding for its resistance is far from assured.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis says Ukraine's battlefield position is improving while Russian forces deteriorate, but rear damage accumulates and funding is uncertain.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Ukraine war will run into a sixth year because Ukraine is gaining at the front while Russia retains hopes of success in the rear. They say Russian forces in Donbas are suffering unprecedented casualties and degrading in quality, leaving them vulnerable in spring, so Ukraine should counterattack once it builds reserves and improves coordination between ground and unmanned forces. In the 'middle strike' zone behind the front, Ukraine currently leads, but its reliance on US-controlled Starshield terminals is a vulnerability, and Russia is experimenting with mesh networks. Deep strikes are where Ukraine is most exposed, as its infrastructure suffers from weaker air defence, while Ukraine is expanding strikes on Russian revenue and defence industry. The authors stress that funding is now a political question, with eight European countries carrying the bill and several key elections in 2027, and they judge that Moscow is trying to disrupt EU funding.
brief.argument: Ukraine's battlefield position is improving while Russia's rear-area strengths and European funding uncertainty mean the war will drag on unless partners guarantee resourcing and Ukraine denies Russia a path to victory.
recommendations: Ukraine should build reserves and strengthen its Army Corps to exploit Russian weakness and counterattack.
Ukraine and partners should develop alternatives to Starshield and supply middle-strike munitions.
Partners should keep funding Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against Russian revenue and defence industry.
Partners must make clear, durable financial commitments to deny the Kremlin its theory of victory.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's own security and defence posture is only indirectly touched, but the piece's warning about European funding fragility and elections in 2027 bears on the regional context for Black Sea and NATO-side planning.

183c9cd71ab31af2.title: The Making of a Global Hunger Crisis
183c9cd71ab31af2.summary: Global conflict has threatened three critical maritime corridors simultaneously, interrupting vital flows of fuel, food, and fertilizer. Now, a record-breaking El Niño event is looking to make things worse. International donors and multinational organizations need to act early to prevent a worst-case scenario.

brief.summary: The authors argue that three maritime chokepoints, the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb and the Black Sea grain corridor, are being disrupted at once by war, while a record El Niño threatens harvests across several regions. They cite rising fuel, freight and insurance costs and falling food and fertilizer supply, with Sudan, Somalia, Central America and Haiti as examples of an emerging hunger crisis. They say forecast emergencies can be acted on early, and that early cash transfers and drought-resistant seed have measurably protected households. They call for rapid donor funding, pre-emptive action tied to forecasts, stronger farming systems, and diplomatic effort to secure shipping lanes ahead of the G20 summit.
brief.argument: Simultaneous chokepoint disruption and a super El Niño threaten to create an unprecedented global hunger crisis, which donors must pre-empt with early, forecast-based action.
recommendations: Surge funding to current emergency response plans in Sudan and Somalia, which are far from fully funded.
Act on forecasts by releasing cash transfers before predicted shocks, not after they arrive.
Strengthen farming systems, including drought-tolerant seed multiplication locally.
Make freedom of navigation a diplomatic priority, with a high-level UN envoy to negotiate safe passage through the chokepoints.

They reject comparisons with the 1945 Yalta summit, contending that the format risks trading Ukraine's interests for a pause in great-power tension and presents a sobering image to Europe and other states that were not consulted. The piece treats the meeting as a signal of shifting influence among the three powers rather than a settlement, and frames the event mainly through what it reveals about American standing. The excerpt available is short, so the full set of arguments and any specific recommendations cannot be confirmed from it.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen meeting serves China's interests and diminishes America's, offering Ukraine risk and Europe a sobering picture of great-power bargaining over its head.

a6e158ab6aa134f4.title: In Shenzhen, weakened giants navigate a dangerous, disorderly world
a6e158ab6aa134f4.summary: When the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents meet on Thursday, weakness rather than strength may prove the most consequential force. The post In Shenzhen, weakened giants navigate a dangerous, disorderly world appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen summit of Trump, Xi and Putin will not produce a new world order but will instead reveal the old order's unraveling without any consensus on a replacement. They contend all three leaders are weakened: Trump by midterm setbacks and fiscal strain, Putin by the drawn-out Ukraine war, and Xi by a faltering economy despite technological gains. Drawing comparisons to Yalta, they say the summit is less promising, since the leaders share no common vision, and more dangerous, because China and Russia seek to replace the post-war US-led order while Washington shows too little determination to defend it. They point to recent US shocks, including the midterm rebuke and the Nvidia leadership change, as likely to intensify US-China tech competition. The piece concludes that the summit's significance lies in whether shared vulnerabilities push the leaders toward accommodation or confrontation.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit will mark the acceleration of the old order's unraveling rather than the birth of a new one, because all three leaders are weakened and China and Russia seek to replace the US-built order without a shared vision.

brief.summary: This is an announcement and preview of a panel dialogue, co-hosted by RUSI and War on the Rocks, on trans-Atlantic defence cooperation after the U.S. midterm elections. The piece presents the discussion as a forward-looking exchange among experts from the UK, continental Europe and the United States, drawing on their experience in the armed forces, diplomacy and foreign policy. It lists the questions the panel will take up: what the midterms mean for U.S. force posture, NATO and support for Ukraine; European investment in defence capabilities; strained supply chains; and whether NATO or the European Union should lead in countering Russian hybrid pressure as European politics shift. The text does not set out a thesis or conclusions, and the body is largely cut off behind a members-only paywall, so the authors' substantive positions are not visible in the excerpt.
brief.argument: The authors frame the post-midterm trans-Atlantic defence agenda as a set of open questions, to be debated rather than settled, on U.S. posture, European capability investment, supply chains and the NATO-EU division of labour against Russian hybrid pressure.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a first-ever U.S.-Chinese-Russian leaders' summit could make trilateral nuclear arms control seem less remote, though substantive breakthroughs are unlikely. They contend China sees the summit mainly as symbolic recognition of its growing strategic power, and that Beijing is unlikely to reverse its nuclear expansion. Their main recommendation is for the leaders to commit to regular, institutionalised nuclear dialogues insulated from wider political disputes, rather than treating talks as bargaining chips. They also propose a joint statement ruling out AI control over nuclear-use decisions, a trilateral missile pre-launch notification agreement, and data-sharing from civilian seismic stations to clarify disputed nuclear tests. On Iran, they see more modest promise in a joint nonproliferation statement, and warn that 'strategic stability' language could embolden lower-level aggression and alarm smaller states.
brief.argument: A trilateral summit is unlikely to yield substantive arms control, but it could open the door to institutionalised, insulated nuclear dialogue and narrower confidence-building steps.
recommendations: Commit to regular, institutionalised nuclear dialogues insulated from broader political tensions, with transparency on progress
Issue a trilateral statement ruling out AI control over nuclear-use decisions
Negotiate a trilateral missile pre-launch notification agreement
Share civilian earthquake-monitoring data to clarify disputed seismic events

brief.summary: The authors argue that China is increasingly using its dominance in production, including rare earths, components, and manufactured goods, as a coercive foreign-policy tool, and that the US alone cannot match this leverage. Because the US accounts for only about a third of global purchases, they propose a 'buyers' club' of market economies, spanning the US, EU, Japan, South Korea, Canada, Australia and others, that would pool consumer demand to counter Chinese export strategies. They say such a bloc could limit fire-sale exports, cushion the costs of rerouting supply chains, and offer protection against retaliation. The authors note early voluntary steps, such as the September framework on steel overcapacity and a narrower coalition on cars, batteries and solar, but they judge these to be toothless and say binding measures would be needed. They also warn that blanket US tariffs on allies undermine cooperation.
brief.argument: Market economies can counter China's weaponised export leverage only by pooling their consumer demand into a binding buyers' club rather than acting unilaterally.
recommendations: Form a buyers' club of major market economies that coordinates trade measures against Chinese overcapacity
Add binding enforcement such as coordinated tariffs, quotas or import bans to the voluntary frameworks
Facilitate investment between members and match subsidies
Avoid blanket tariffs on allies so they have reason to join

f55fd302b3845829.title: The Real Reason Why Everything Seems to Be Crashing
f55fd302b3845829.summary: To understand the recent spate of tech system failures, we need to turn a Silicon Valley adage on its head. Instead of “move fast and break things,” think more “move fast and fix things, but still break them inadvertently.”

brief.summary: The author argues that a recent run of high-profile tech outages (Microsoft, an FAA ground stop, banking and Apple services, and the NSA's NSANet) appears to have unconnected technical causes rather than hostile cyberattacks, with U.S. officials ruling out adversary involvement. He examines two AI-related explanations: a newly installed AI-supported FAA air traffic tool (which officials say was not connected to core systems, with the FAA blaming a new router), and the indirect effect of AI tools finding bugs in widely used software like PHP and Java, which pushes firms to patch quickly and sometimes causes new failures. He frames this as a shift from 'move fast and break things' to 'move fast and fix things, but still break them inadvertently.' He notes that Iran-linked IRGC hackers have targeted operational technology during the war with Tehran, and that critical infrastructure is vulnerable, but says the recent outages do not look like that. He concludes that dependence on complex systems will grow as AI is integrated with legacy software, and that clear, timely official communication matters because people will see patterns where none exist.
brief.argument: The recent system failures look like inadvertent consequences of AI-accelerated patching and integration rather than cyberattacks, but they expose how dependent society is on fragile complex systems.
recommendations: Provide clear, timely communication from technology platforms and government about what they know
Expect instability to persist as new AI systems are integrated with legacy software

brief.summary: The authors argue that COP31 in Antalya missed a chance to treat food security as a geopolitical issue, focusing instead on long-established topics such as the food-water-climate nexus and women farmers' financing. They contend food weaponization, the deliberate manipulation of food access or supplies, is under-addressed despite a 2018 UN Security Council condemnation of starvation as a method of war. Drawing on fertilizer shocks from the Iran war, Hormuz disruptions, Russian attacks on Black Sea grain infrastructure and a possible strong El Niño, they say climate shocks make the system more fragile. The author calls for linking trade coercion, wartime starvation and food as a long-range weapon, closing the gap between norms and enforcement, and building early-warning tools. A UN disaster risk financing platform is noted as one positive step.
brief.argument: COP31 failed to treat food weaponization as a geopolitical security issue, and the gap between international norms and enforcement needs closing.
recommendations: Develop a strategic food security roadmap toward COP32 that links resilience to food weaponization
Converge policy discussions on trade coercion, wartime starvation and food as a long-range weapon
Expand early-warning indicators for droughts and connect climate adaptation with conflict-prevention bodies
Close the gap between rhetorical commitments and enforcement against food weaponization

db9c3c256f2c7bb2.title: Donald Tusk, Chris Wright, and Miłosz Motyka on the mindset shift needed across the energy system
db9c3c256f2c7bb2.summary: The three leaders spoke at the seventh Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation, making the case for more energy production as supplies tighten and prices skyrocket. The post Donald Tusk, Chris Wright, and Miłosz Motyka on the mindset shift needed across the energy system appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Donald Tusk and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright call for more energy production at a transatlantic energy cooperation forum.

brief.summary: The authors report on the seventh Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation ministerial in Warsaw, where Polish PM Donald Tusk, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Polish Energy Minister Miłosz Motyka argued for a shift toward pragmatic energy policy. Tusk framed transatlantic energy cooperation as part of a strategic alliance between Poland, Europe and the United States, insisting that ideology should not override energy-source logic as supplies tighten and prices rise. Wright described energy cooperation as a strategic partnership rather than a commercial matter, and Motyka stressed faster build-out of production, nuclear power and LNG diversification through Poland as a gateway for US gas. Motyka also pressed the EU to postpone its Emissions Trading System and to revise nuclear taxonomy rules, and Tusk called for coordinated support for Ukraine's energy system during winter.
brief.argument: Energy security in a disrupted world requires pragmatic, non-ideological choices and deeper US-European energy partnership, including expanded nuclear and LNG capacity.
recommendations: Expand energy production faster by cutting bureaucratic delays
Postpone the EU Emissions Trading System to ease consumer costs
Change the EU taxonomy so more nuclear activities qualify as green
Coordinate US and European support for Ukraine's energy infrastructure over winter

7122c5a4127150d2.title: Libya’s reunification and path to democracy start with fixing its budget
7122c5a4127150d2.summary: A recent Atlantic Council roundtable with Libyan officials, Italian policymakers, and international experts and analysts examined UN and US efforts to reunite the country. The post Libya’s reunification and path to democracy start with fixing its budget appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that Libya's reunification and democratic transition should start with fixing its divided public budget. After a roundtable in Rome, they describe how the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity pushed for a political rather than purely technocratic approach to spending, leading to an April unified financial framework under which the Central Bank sets total funding and development spending is distributed geographically. They say the US-backed initiative helped by narrowing negotiations to the two de facto authorities. Italian participants prioritised implementation, fiscal transparency and Central Bank capacity, and stressed elections, while Algerian participants insisted on a Libyan-led political solution and warned first of foreign interference, militias and weapons flows, including Russian pressure. Participants rejected partition, favoured parliamentary over presidential elections, and called for elections without further delay.
brief.argument: Libya's reunification and democratic path should begin with a unified, transparent public budget, with elections held without further delay and no partition.
recommendations: Implement the April unified budget framework with fiscal discipline, transparency and effective oversight of public resources.
Deepen support for the Central Bank of Libya and other technical bodies.
Hold parliamentary rather than presidential elections without further delay.
Address internal security and foreign interference before or alongside political steps.

8d00a676ec48e843.title: Dispatch from Kyiv: Let Ukraine strike Russia’s missile launchers at the source
8d00a676ec48e843.summary: Russia's missile production vastly outpaces the output of interceptors for Ukraine and by the United States—an issue that should concern militaries around the world. The post Dispatch from Kyiv: Let Ukraine strike Russia’s missile launchers at the source appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council dispatch argues Ukraine should strike Russian missile launchers at source given Russia's interceptor shortfall.

brief.summary: The authors, writing from Kyiv, argue that Ukraine's cities are being battered by Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones that Ukraine lacks the interceptors to stop at scale. They describe Russia's missile output as far outpacing Western interceptor production, and say Starshield connectivity limits imposed since October have hampered Ukrainian drones at the front and against Shaheds. To counter this, they propose that Ukraine be allowed to use Starshield up to about 300 km inside Russia to strike mobile missile launchers before they fire, and that Western partners approve transfers of existing Patriot interceptors now. They present the Starshield access as a low-cost step that could also push Moscow toward negotiations.
brief.argument: Ukraine can only protect its cities this winter if it is allowed to hit Russian missile launchers at the source and gets Patriot interceptors and unrestricted Starshield access now.
recommendations: Lift the Starshield speed cap over occupied Ukraine.
Authorise Ukraine's use of Starshield up to about 300 km inside Russia to strike a jointly approved list of missile launchers and launch sites, with joint oversight and terminal whitelisting.
Press allies to transfer existing Patriot interceptors to Kyiv now, with US approval for European stock transfers.
Trade the Starshield access for a pause on Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy assets.
brief.turkey: Starshield and Patriot access decisions in Washington and European capitals shape the air-defence and satellite-communications environment that Türkiye's own defence planning and its Black Sea neighbourhood depend on.

664f38bd2f824af3.title: Upheaval in the Greater North African Security Complex demands a new transatlantic policy approach
664f38bd2f824af3.summary: A recent Atlantic Council roundtable brought together Italian policymakers, international experts, and analysts to examine interconnected security dynamics across North Africa, the Sahel, and the Red Sea. The post Upheaval in the Greater North African Security Complex demands a new transatlantic policy approach appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that North Africa, the Sahel, the Red Sea and Egypt now form a single interlocking security complex, and that Western policy has not kept pace. They describe a Maghreb split into a Moroccan bloc, aligned with the US, France, Israel and the UAE, and a more defensive Algerian bloc that has raised military spending and widened its legal scope for operations abroad. In the Sahel they say militancy is driven mainly by political exclusion rather than religion, and that heavy European intervention worsened security and fed the coups. They present Turkey as a rising arms exporter and naval power, and argue its NATO membership and Mecca defence pact are compatible. They also describe Egypt as a pivotal but strained actor, and call for a renewed transatlantic partnership with it.
brief.argument: The authors argue that the Maghreb rivalry, Sahel instability, Red Sea and Egyptian pressures form one Greater North African Security Complex that requires a new transatlantic policy approach.
recommendations: Treat Algeria as the central interlocutor for any renewed Sahel negotiations rather than Morocco.
Anchor Egypt in maritime and regional security frameworks and link international support to reforms.
Engage Sahel juntas on more equal, transactional terms while keeping Europe's human rights role.
brief.turkey: The authors present Türkiye as a major drone exporter and emerging blue-water naval power, training large numbers of Somali soldiers, and see no conflict between its NATO membership and the Mecca defence pact.

afe66ea5a22c9f86.summary: Xi-Trump-Putin meet: why Shenzhen won't be a Yalta 2.0 newspress_en Wed, 11/18/2026 - 17:48 Politics In the Chinese city of Shenzhen, President Xi Jinping is hosting US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit. Some analysts are likening the 19 November 2026 meeting to the Yalta Conference of 1945, when the leaders of America, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed how to carve up Europe after the Second World War. Xi, Trump, and…

ai.sum: Xi Jinping is hosting Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in a trilateral summit in Shenzhen on 19 November 2026.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen summit of Xi, Trump and Putin will not resemble the 1945 Yalta Conference and will not settle a new world order. They trace Trump's failed attempt to pull Moscow away from Beijing, the Sino-US détente that has produced shared interests over Iran and Hormuz, and Washington's softening toward Putin, including a Russian diesel deal and easing on Starshield for Ukraine. They then examine how Trump's midterm losses leave him a domestic 'lame duck' but still able to act on foreign policy, while Congress may press harder on Taiwan and chips. Their core point is that Xi has little freedom to deliver what Trump wants, especially on Iran and Ukraine, since Beijing wants to keep its leverage over Moscow. The authors say Yalta comparisons miss that the three leaders are not allies with a shared postwar design, and that for Xi the summit's main gain may simply be holding it.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit is unlikely to set a new international order because Xi lacks the freedom and the interests to deliver big concessions, and the leaders are not allies with a shared design like Yalta's.

b1d32a28f5837ef4.summary: The dominance of the U.S. dollar is a crucial source of American global power. The dollar’s widespread use, strength, and reliability provide major economic advantages for the United States, enable U.S. sanctions to have real bite, and significantly boost U.S. influence abroad. For America’s adversaries — as well as for many other countries that view Washington with some skepticism — dependence on the dollar comes with significant risks. Over the years, various proposals to…

brief.summary: The piece, a War on the Rocks roundtable, asks whether countries such as China can effectively reduce reliance on the US dollar through a rival currency or alternative payment systems. The authors separate the dollar's role as a store of national wealth, which they treat as entrenched, from its role in making payments, which they see as increasingly contestable. They point to the BRICS push for cross-border payment systems, the rise of China, non-dollar stablecoins and new payment networks as pressures on dollar payment dominance. The text available is only the opening portion; the full analysis of each expert's answer sits behind the members-only paywall, so the specific conclusions of the five contributors cannot be reported here.
brief.argument: The dollar's role as a store of wealth is entrenched, while its payments dominance is increasingly contestable as middle powers seek non-dollar 'payment optionality'.

brief.summary: The author argues that economic hardship is becoming a serious threat to confidence in Syria's post-Assad transition. Drawing on conversations across Syria, he finds that people, including many who lost relatives under Assad, are relieved the regime has ended but increasingly frustrated by the cost of living and miss the earlier affordability of daily life. He points to a Friday sermon in Idlib by an outspoken Assad critic, which reportedly voiced such comparisons, as evidence that frustration now reaches the new authorities' political heartland. The authors stress that the public focus on whether the preacher sympathised with Assad obscures the more consequential warning about economic grievances eroding trust in the transition.
brief.argument: Economic hardship, rather than nostalgia for Assad, is becoming a serious threat to confidence in Syria's transition, and it is now voiced openly even in Idlib.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Gulf states are extending economic diversification from growth sources to where essential resources are stored and accessed. The 2026 Hormuz disruption showed that bypass pipelines and financial buffers cannot secure revenues or market access alone, and that Asian buyers may shift supply if Gulf cargoes stop for weeks. Asia is emerging as the centre of Gulf overseas reserves, with Japan and South Korea providing operational precedents. The piece distinguishes true strategic reserves, which carry emergency access rights, from commercial hubs that earn throughput revenue without such rights. It sets out four investment models, from commercial leasing to co-developed hubs, and points to African ports such as Mombasa as a further route, while noting that several of these projects remain unconfirmed or preliminary.
brief.argument: Gulf producers are storing oil abroad, especially in Asia, to protect market access and commercial relationships as well as to keep reserves against supply shocks.

ai.sum: Analysis asks whether US aid to Egypt survives fallout from midterms, after Trump said he agreed with Netanyahu to end US defence aid to Israel.

brief.summary: The authors examine whether US aid to Egypt will survive political fallout from the midterm elections. They argue that Egypt's aid is anchored in the 1978 Camp David Accords and the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty, so Cairo fears that any cut to aid for Israel would logically extend to Egypt. They note that Democrats gaining control of Congress has brought renewed scrutiny of foreign military assistance, with some lawmakers calling for cuts, citing Egypt's ties with Russia and China and its crackdown on independent media. Against this, they point to pragmatic signals from Washington: Secretary Rubio's praise of Egypt as a reliable partner and the White House's warm relationship with Sisi, which suggest a possible gap between Congress and the executive. Proponents of continued aid cite Egypt's role in preserving the peace with Israel, securing Suez and Red Sea shipping, brokering the Gaza ceasefire and serving as the main gateway for humanitarian aid.
brief.argument: US aid to Egypt is at risk from congressional reappraisal of military assistance, but the executive branch's pragmatic backing and Egypt's regional roles may sustain it.
recommendations: Egypt's foreign minister should lobby lawmakers in Washington to preserve the aid.
Cairo should keep pushing for the next phases of the Gaza ceasefire plan and help with reconstruction.
Washington should weigh Egypt's role in Suez, Red Sea security and the Eastern Mediterranean when reviewing aid.
brief.turkey: A cut to US aid to Egypt would reshape the regional balance around Israel, Gaza and the Red Sea, bearing on Türkiye's own calculations in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Gaza file.

Trump's bid to pull Moscow away from Beijing has largely failed, and his setbacks on Ukraine and tariffs have pushed him toward easing tensions with China while courting Putin. Shared interests on Iran and Hormuz have strengthened US-China stability. Trump is weakened at home after the midterms, but retains room to act in foreign policy. Xi has little reason to offer concessions on Ukraine, Iran or nuclear arms, and Beijing wants to keep the initiative with Moscow. The authors stress that the 2026 setting differs sharply from 1945: there is no wartime alliance and the leaders' priorities diverge. For Xi, the summit may matter mainly as a diplomatic showcase.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit will not reshape the international order like Yalta did, because the three leaders lack a shared alliance and their priorities and constraints diverge.

f5288c38ed65e282.title: The Ground Beneath the Cloud: Dispersion and Dependency in the Digital Age
f5288c38ed65e282.summary: Commercial cloud architecture has made digital infrastructure more resilient to localized disruption. Geographic dispersion, workload migration, and failover have allowed providers to preserve access in instances of degradation or even destruction. Yet, underpinning this resiliency are interlocking dependencies on access to energy, supply chains, and governing bodies that extend well beyond the data centers hosting the commercial cloud. The United States is building digital…

brief.summary: The author argues that commercial cloud dispersion protects data only up to a point, because failover depends on energy grids, subsea fibre, transformers, critical minerals and host-government rules that no hyperscaler controls. He points to the 2026 Iranian strikes on AWS facilities in Bahrain and the UAE, where physical damage eventually exceeded regional redundancy, and to data-residency laws that can make failover illegal. Scaling data centres also multiplies vulnerable nodes such as substations and cable routes, and China's leverage over gallium and other minerals adds supply risk. The authors propose state-coordinated measures: a Commercial Compute Reserve with crisis priority, a standalone critical infrastructure sector for data centres, and physical resilience standards written into government cloud contracts. They frame these as a joint doctrine between the Pentagon and industry.
brief.argument: Cloud resilience rests on physical, supply-chain and governance dependencies that individual hyperscalers cannot control, so the US needs state-coordinated doctrine to protect the infrastructure beneath the cloud.
recommendations: Establish a Department of Defense Commercial Compute Reserve with crisis priority, backed by indemnification and Defense Production Act authorities.
Designate data centres as a standalone critical infrastructure sector with a sector risk management agency and mandatory minimum security requirements.
Write physical resilience standards against deliberate attack into government and classified cloud regions and future Unified Cloud Marketplace task orders.
Offer expedited power and permitting on federal sites in exchange for reserve participation.

519b61967a392487.title: Six Experts on the Significance of Trump, Xi, and Putin’s First Trilateral Meeting
519b61967a392487.summary: A first-ever trilateral summit put the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia in one room as the Ukraine war and the U.S.-China trade truce loom. CFR experts explore what came out of the meeting and what comes next.

ai.sum: Experts analyse the significance and outcomes of the first trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.

brief.summary: A CFR roundtable by six experts assesses the first trilateral summit of Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen. The authors broadly agree the meeting was largely symbolic: optics outweighed substance, and the joint declaration said nothing on Ukraine, Taiwan or Iran. Froman stresses that the Manila leg and Quad supply-chain deals mattered more for US standing. Doshi argues Beijing gained symbolic leverage while its rare-earth squeeze and coercion of Japan and the Philippines show it is using the detente as a tactical pause. Graham sees Putin gaining great-power photo validation without progress on territory or security guarantees. Fix and Dumbacher treat the pledge to talk on nuclear risk as a modest opening, with Dumbacher noting it lacks the verification of past treaties. McGuire finds the trade truce fragile, with both sides undermining it, and welcomes new US AI chip export enforcement. The piece closes with watch items: the Miami G20, the January 10, 2027 truce expiry, further Ukraine talks, and a possible Russian or Chinese role on Iran.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen trilateral was mainly a symbolic display of great-power status that produced little of substance on arms control, Ukraine or trade, and the US-China truce is fragile.
recommendations: Treat the nuclear risk-reduction dialogue as a starting point and build lower-level preparation before expecting arms control outcomes.
Keep US export controls on advanced AI chips as a tool to preserve US leadership, and be ready to escalate economically if China retaliates.
Use the G20 meeting in Miami to build on any Shenzhen understandings and to address the truce expiry.
Reassure European allies that great-power summitry does not mean a new Yalta-style division of spheres.
brief.turkey: Türkiye should note the signal that Washington may prioritise great-power engagement over allies, and that nuclear-risk talks could shape how regional powers think about hedging.

abb4ad8be5511e95.title: Boom or Bubble? Understanding AI and the U.S. Economy
abb4ad8be5511e95.summary: Investments in artificial intelligence (AI) have powered much of the U.S. stock market’s gains in recent years. But growing debt and public backlash are making investors wary that the AI boom could go bust, threatening the U.S. economy and its ability to compete with China.

brief.summary: The authors argue that AI investment has become the largest investment boom in U.S. history and has powered much of recent stock market gains and growth, though its productivity payoff remains unclear. They present mixed evidence on whether it is a bubble: hyperscalers now spend more than they earn, debt and circular financing are rising, and Nvidia's market value fell sharply after its CEO's departure. They distinguish AI from past bubbles by pointing to larger, more profitable firms and the multipurpose nature of the technology. Constraints on power, land, skilled labour and imported inputs could slow the build-out, and the authors frame U.S. competition with China around supply-chain dependence on East Asia and the U.S. edge in AI safety and security. They conclude that it is too early to call the boom a bubble.
brief.argument: The AI investment boom is historically unprecedented and has propped up U.S. growth, but rising debt, weak revenues and constrained supply could make it unsustainable, though its underlying technology is likely durable.

eac88cadc074ad7a.title: Democrats Should Repurpose, Not Retire, the China Select Committee
eac88cadc074ad7a.summary: The new House majority will decide in January whether to renew the Select Committee on China. Democrats should keep the committee and give it a new mandate: domestic renewal, defense against a second China Shock, human rights, allied scale, and a workable path to cooperation.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the incoming House majority should renew the House Select Committee on China rather than let it lapse, but repurpose it around five pillars: American domestic renewal, defence against a second China Shock of subsidised Chinese exports, restoring human rights as a policy priority, building allied scale, and a realistic approach to cooperation with China on issues like AI, climate and health. They contend the committee is distinct because it is wholly made up of members of Congress, can view China policy across jurisdictions, and has already helped move bipartisan measures such as outbound-investment rules and the BIOSECURE Act. They frame the aim as managing competition while securing US interests and avoiding demagogy and anti-Asian racism, and suggest the committee's name and rhetoric could be adjusted to reflect this.
brief.argument: The House should renew the China Select Committee and give it a Democratic-led mandate centred on domestic renewal, economic defence, human rights, allied scale and managed cooperation with China.
recommendations: Renew the Select Committee in January and repurpose it around five pillars rather than letting it lapse
Make the second China Shock, from subsidised Chinese exports, its first major inquiry, identifying exposed industries and regions
Elevate human rights across trade, technology, investment and pension-fund decisions
Treat allied coordination as a central focus, turning alliances into platforms for pooled industrial and technological capacity

a56c1101cd7542b2.title: The 1863 Gettysburg Address
a56c1101cd7542b2.summary: President Abraham Lincoln’s brief remarks dedicating the Soldiers’ National Cemetery at Gettysburg provided a defining statement of America’s democratic ideals.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for the Council on Foreign Relations, revisit Lincoln's 1863 Gettysburg Address, delivered at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery four months after the battle. They note that Lincoln spoke only two minutes after Edward Everett's two-hour oration, and that early press reactions were mixed, with one paper calling it a gem and another dismissing it. The piece argues that history has firmly sided with the favourable verdict, and describes how scholars have since studied the surviving drafts, the speech's composition, and its intellectual sources. The text is a historical retrospective on American democratic ideals rather than a policy analysis, and it offers no policy recommendations. It is a republished essay marking the United States' 250th anniversary.
brief.argument: Lincoln's brief Gettysburg Address defined America's democratic ideals and has earned its lasting reputation as one of the greatest speeches ever delivered.

brief.summary: Speaking at a Warsaw conference on transatlantic energy cooperation, Polish Energy Minister Miłosz Motyka argues that Central and Eastern Europe must become a growth engine, and that cheap, available energy and deregulation are needed for Europe to keep its industrial competitiveness. The transcript records speeches rather than a systematic analysis, so the arguments are largely rhetorical.
brief.argument: Europe's security and growth depend on cheap, abundant energy, which the authors say requires nuclear expansion, US natural gas and LNG, and deregulation rather than climate-driven restrictions.

The ministers call for joint European purchasing, better cross-border transport such as the Vertical Corridor, protection of energy infrastructure against hybrid threats like drones, sabotage and cyberattacks, and a more pragmatic approach to EU sustainability targets alongside renewables, nuclear and baseload capacity.
brief.argument: Europe's energy ministers argue that the break with Russian gas is irreversible and that resilience now depends on diversification, joint purchasing, infrastructure protection and baseload capacity.

Improve cross-border gas transport infrastructure, such as the Vertical Corridor, so supplies reach all member states

3c5f0b385ebe0d5b.title: The foresight brief: Chokepoints past, present, and future
3c5f0b385ebe0d5b.summary: Maritime straits, canals, ports, rivers, subsea cables, data centers, and cloud infrastructure are concentrated points of connection. Yet their significance is changing as supply chains evolve, geopolitical competition intensifies, and climate change reshapes the physical world. The post The foresight brief: Chokepoints past, present, and future appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that chokepoints, strategically important connectors with few or no alternatives, remain central to the global economy even as it becomes more digital. They define a chokepoint by both the volume it carries and the consequences of its disruption, with the 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz offered as the illustrative case. They contend that maritime straits, canals, ports, subsea cables and data centres all concentrate influence and vulnerability, so disruption at one point cascades across global systems. The brief says these vulnerabilities are shifting as supply chains change, great-power competition intensifies and climate change alters the physical world, with possible new exposure in digital infrastructure and perhaps space. For business leaders, the authors frame chokepoints as revealing strategic dependencies that can be assessed, hedged and turned into opportunities for investment and cooperation.
brief.argument: Chokepoints concentrate influence and vulnerability, so leaders must map the chokepoints their objectives depend on and assess where disruption would constrain their options.
recommendations: Identify the chokepoints on which the organisation's objectives depend
Assess where disruption at those points could constrain options
Map where critical systems are concentrated and how they interact under stress
Identify alternatives and strengthen capacity to act before disruption occurs
brief.turkey: Türkiye's Bosphorus and Dardanelles and its role in energy and cable routes make the framework directly relevant to its exposure to chokepoint disruption, though the brief does not address Türkiye specifically.

brief.argument: The Kremlin's growing use of disposable mercenaries for sub-threshold attacks in Europe lowers perceived risk and could eventually trigger a catastrophic incident like MH17.

af80ddf5a35baedf.title: Toplines: Why and how the United States and its allies should prepare for a limited nuclear attack
af80ddf5a35baedf.summary: How should the United States and its allies prepare for a limited nuclear attack, and why? An expert tabletop exercise gaming out scenarios in which North Korea might launch such an attack offered insights. The post Toplines: Why and how the United States and its allies should prepare for a limited nuclear attack appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the United States and its allies are insufficiently prepared for a limited nuclear attack (LNA) by North Korea, which they judge increasingly likely over the next decade as its warheads and delivery systems diversify. They attribute the gap partly to cognitive and organisational reluctance to think about nuclear war. Their remedies centre on a shared conceptual understanding of LNA placed within conventional-nuclear integration, and on psychological and political resilience, since the effects of an attack could far exceed its physical damage. They also call for a deliberate influence campaign to deter such attacks, and for mitigating alliance politics, declaratory policy and capability shortfalls that limit response options. The study draws on engagements with over 150 stakeholders, workshops and a multinational tabletop exercise, using North Korea as the case.
brief.argument: The United States and its allies must prepare for, and communicate about, limited nuclear attacks by North Korea, because deterrence and resilience are currently insufficient for a risk they judge growing.
recommendations: Develop and disseminate tailored products on LNA risks and adversary capabilities for US and allied decision-makers.
Establish unclassified education and training curricula on LNA effects, alongside a public booklet on effects and mitigation.
Sponsor official and mixed-track convenings to build a shared, flexible conceptualisation of LNA within conventional-nuclear integration.
Engage potential target states such as South Korea and adjust posture and capabilities to provide flexible, resilient response options.

715b89b8157c44f4.title: Estonia has a chance to reboot the Ukraine Recovery Conference

ai.sum: Analysis argues Estonia's 2027 Ukraine Recovery Conference in Tallinn could shift from signing ceremonies to substantive discussion of Ukraine's future.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 2027 Ukraine Recovery Conference in Tallinn, moved to January, can be a chance to reset the series. They trace how the conference began as a Ukraine Reform Conference, was renamed for recovery after 2022, and drifted toward signing ceremonies and investment promotion while the war continued. They say success is now measured by deal counts, while Ukraine's real bottlenecks are strategic planning, project preparation and local government capacity, worsened by the dismantling of USAID. They propose using Tallinn as the start of a year-long, Ukrainian-led effort with thematic working sessions, a spring reform meeting, a summer investment meeting and a year-end review. They present Estonia's own post-Soviet transition and digital governance record as a basis for this role, and see resilience and recovery as inseparable.
brief.argument: Tallinn's URC should move away from signing ceremonies and toward building Ukraine's institutional capacity to plan, prepare and deliver recovery and EU integration, starting as a year-long process.
recommendations: Start the January Tallinn meeting as the opening of a year-long, Ukrainian-led effort with clear priorities.
Identify the main bottlenecks first (strategic planning, project preparation, procurement, local government capacity) before adding initiatives.
Use targeted technical assistance and temporary staff working alongside Ukrainian counterparts to fill gaps.
Hold spring reform and summer investment working sessions and a year-end review, with Nordic-Baltic, EU, IFI and bilateral partners contributing.

They favour enabling regional partners to take more constructive security roles since 9/11, with Washington shifting from guarantor to facilitator and integrator. The US should still defend its enduring interests (freedom of navigation, nonproliferation, counterterrorism) independently, but jointly with partners and without subcontracting security to them or to China. brief.argument: US Middle East posture should be reshaped around capability, access and specialisation, with partners taking greater security responsibility, rather than merely cut or relocated.
recommendations: Shift the US role from security guardian or guarantor to facilitator and integrator of regional partners.
Prioritise capability, access and specialisation over footprint, capacity and dispersion in force posture.

The authors judge that Tehran has shown it can absorb pressure and resists major concessions. They warn that Iran has options, such as rebuilding missile and drone stocks, reviving its nuclear programme, escalating regional attacks, cyber operations, and gray-zone activity in Europe and North America. Any of these could prompt renewed US strikes, and each side reads concessions as weakness. The text is a members-only excerpt, so further recommendations are not visible.
brief.argument: Without a clear US objective, economic pressure on Iran is unlikely to produce concessions, and Tehran has options that could push the two sides back toward major military strikes.

77d15e4802a57569.title: The Senate Rejects the Treaty of Versailles
77d15e4802a57569.summary: The defeat of President Woodrow Wilson’s plan for a League of Nations highlighted the power of the Senate and the dangers of refusing to compromise.

ai.sum: A historical CFR piece recounts the US Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles and Wilson's League of Nations.

brief.summary: The authors, writing as a CFR retrospective on the 1919 Senate rejection of the Treaty of Versailles, trace how Woodrow Wilson moved from neutrality to war and then to championing a League of Nations as the centrepiece of the peace. They argue that Wilson's domestic political missteps, including his appeal to voters before the 1918 midterms, cost Democrats control of Congress and hardened Republican opposition. They describe Senate chair Henry Cabot Lodge delaying the treaty and drafting fourteen reservations, while Wilson refused to compromise and then suffered a stroke. The piece characterises the debate as one over the form of internationalism rather than a simple isolationist-versus-internationalist split. The authors conclude that US non-participation weakened the League and that the lesson of the episode shaped American foreign policy for the following eight decades. It is a historical essay with no explicit policy recommendations.
brief.argument: The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles resulted from Wilson's refusal to compromise and his domestic political miscalculations, and it shaped US engagement with the world for decades.

7c88fa8b9f96aa0a.summary: In the Shenzhen summit with Trump and Xi, Putin got the propaganda victory he wanted without having to make any concessions on Ukraine. The post Putin didn’t get his Yalta, but he’s happy nonetheless appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Commentary says Putin gained a propaganda win at the Shenzhen summit with Trump and Xi without conceding on Ukraine.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen trilateral summit among Putin, Xi and Trump, though far from the Yalta-style gathering Putin had wanted, gave him a valuable image of normalcy and friendship with the US president. They read the joint declaration as tailored to Russian concerns: its language on the ICC, nuclear war, oil flows and the UN serves Putin's interests, while Ukraine is not mentioned. They see Xi placing Putin as a junior partner, but argue that Putin is nonetheless content. The authors contend that Putin gains a political signal to the Russian elite that he cannot be isolated, and that Trump's reluctance to sanction Russian oil exports effectively secures his economy. They conclude that Putin is not moving toward a peace settlement and sees no reason to compromise with a US administration he regards as a lame duck.
brief.argument: Putin gained a major symbolic and economic win from the Shenzhen summit without making any concessions on Ukraine or peace.

441ead00bcbad52f.title: What the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting actually achieved
441ead00bcbad52f.summary: Our experts unpack what Trump, Xi, and Putin gained from their summit and what their declaration means for the global order. The post What the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting actually achieved appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts analysed the gains and implications of a Trump, Xi and Putin summit and its declaration.

brief.summary: The authors, Atlantic Council experts, argue that the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting in Shenzhen was mostly image and little substance. They say Beijing shaped the narrative through a four-point "declaration toward peace". They see one modest gain in the reaffirmation that a nuclear war cannot be won, and that China's inclusion could be built on. They warn that China's nuclear build-up continues, and that the leaders' stance on the ICC threatens its foundations and moves away from US support for accountability. They read the UN reform call as serving Beijing's push against Western values, and the oil production point as likely to favour Russia by undermining sanctions. Xi gains a picture of China in the driver's seat, Putin gains equal great-power standing, and Trump misses a chance to advance a free-world agenda. The authors also contrast the summit with the Berlin Coalition of the Willing meeting on Ukraine.
brief.argument: The authors argue that the Trump-Putin-Xi summit was all image and little substance, with its declaration advancing Beijing's narrative, weakening ICC accountability, and easing pressure on Russian oil sales.
recommendations: The US president should back the Berlin Coalition of the Willing meeting rather than pursue photo opportunities with Putin.
Build on the nuclear-war reaffirmation by bringing China further into nuclear-arms discussions.
UN reform should promote accountability and equal voices among states rather than consolidate great-power power.
brief.turkey: The summit's signals on Russian oil sanctions and great-power bargaining over Ukraine bear on Türkiye's energy and Black Sea calculations, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

a4b06227be3c8f4a.title: The US didn’t have a strong plan for the Shenzhen summit. It showed.
a4b06227be3c8f4a.summary: The leaders’ trilateral meeting in Shenzhen ended up benefiting Beijing and Moscow at the expense of Washington. The post The US didn’t have a strong plan for the Shenzhen summit. It showed. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Analysis says the Shenzhen trilateral summit benefited Beijing and Moscow at Washington's expense.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the United States went into the Shenzhen trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin without a clear plan, and so was used to lend legitimacy to China and Russia. They say Trump rests his approach on three misconceptions: that Xi and Putin like him, that Chinese pageantry benefits Washington, and that Sino-Russian ties will loosen because they 'like Trump'. The summit produced a four-point declaration that, in their reading, mostly serves Chinese and Russian aims, such as UN reform, more fossil fuel production and immunity for heads of state from the ICC. The one point they think Washington added, a dialogue on nuclear risk, is in their view empty and buys Beijing time while its arsenal grows. They conclude that the US left with nothing concrete, while the images will shape how allies view their ties with Washington, and they urge focus on partners who want to work with the US rather than on splitting China and Russia.
brief.argument: The US walked into the Shenzhen summit without a strong plan, and the trilateral format let Beijing and Moscow gain image and substance at American expense.
recommendations: Enter leader-level meetings with authoritarian rivals only with a clear, specific plan and concrete objectives
Seek tangible commitments, such as reliable rare earth supply for US companies, rather than accepting pageantry
Stop spending effort trying to drive China and Russia apart and focus on allies who want to work with the US
Treat empty dialogue offers on nuclear risk as stalling tactics unless they come with verifiable steps
brief.turkey: The summit's images and the Sino-Russian-US framing bear on how Ankara reads US reliability and great-power bargaining, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.
