4381742c79742f14.title: Lessons from Brazil and Peru on how to build AI-ready institutions across Latin America
4381742c79742f14.summary: Brazil and Peru offer early blueprints for AI regulation in Latin America: one for building regulatory institutions before legislation is in place, and another for turning AI laws into effective governance. The post Lessons from Brazil and Peru on how to build AI-ready institutions across Latin America appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council examines how Brazil and Peru are building AI regulatory institutions and governance frameworks.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Latin American AI governance is colliding with institutional limits, since imported European-style regulatory models must be translated into clear authority, operational capacity and accountability at home. They compare two cases. Brazil is building institutional architecture before its general AI law is settled, strengthening its data protection authority into a full regulator and showing how the electoral court acted as an interim AI regulator in the 2026 elections. Peru has passed a general AI law and implementing regulations that divide enforcement among existing bodies, but they warn its agencies may lack budget and bandwidth to enforce. The authors frame three tests for AI readiness: clear authority, capacity to absorb mandates, and mechanisms to detect and correct failure. They conclude that regulation is only one part of readiness and must be developed alongside institutions.
brief.argument: Latin American AI governance will be hollow unless institutional authority, operational capacity and accountability are built alongside regulation, as the Brazil and Peru cases show.
recommendations: Clearly define the processes, roles and responsibilities of actors across the data lifecycle, drawing on the OAS MIGDIA framework before comprehensive AI law exists.
Empower existing judicial institutions to act as interim regulators for specific risks while an independent AI regulator is established.
Set up efficient inter-agency communication channels and sector-based enforcement responsibilities to ensure accountability.
Scale institutional resources as regulatory responsibilities expand, and build transparency through reporting indicators on digital government capacity.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Ukraine's long-range drone strikes have sharply cut Russian oil refining, with a 45 percent drop cited from Reuters and a higher figure from Zelenskyy. Their central puzzle is why there are not more such drones, and they answer that money, not engineering or industrial capacity, is the constraint. They say Ukraine's defence sector now has large excess capacity, with officials estimating that much of it is unused or uncontracted, while Kyiv spends about 40 percent of GDP on defence, largely on personnel. They highlight the 'Danish model', in which donors pay Ukrainian manufacturers directly, and argue that Ukrainian drones are cheap and combat-tested. They acknowledge corruption concerns and call for audits, and note dependence on imported engines and electronics, which joint ventures with European partners could address.
brief.argument: Money, rather than industrial capacity, is what limits Ukraine's drone output, so Kyiv's partners should fund Ukrainian domestic production.
recommendations: Direct donor funding to Ukrainian defence manufacturers through the Danish model
Pair funding with audits and transparency safeguards against corruption
Form joint ventures with European partners to secure imported components and move production out of Russian strike range
Channel part of NATO allies' increased defence budgets into Ukrainian production

brief.summary: The author argues that Putin has scored two diplomatic wins in ten days: the Abu Dhabi talks, where a prisoner exchange was agreed and US negotiators echoed Russian framing of the war's origins, and the Shenzhen meeting with Xi and Trump. She describes a repeating pattern since early 2025 in which US initiatives drift toward Russian positions, and Europe responds reactively with envoys and symbolic counterweights. Since the new US Congress from January will constrain Trump's room for manoeuvre and Ukraine has shown it can pressure Russia militarily, she contends Europe can shape the process. She says Europe should stop posing as a mediator, since it is a party, and should define clear war-end goals, a stable ceasefire first, and a strategy built on strengthening Ukraine on the battlefield.
brief.argument: Europe must stop reacting to US-Russia dealmaking and become a party that shapes the Ukraine negotiations, starting from clear goals and a strategy to strengthen Ukraine.

brief.summary: The authors examine the Democratic takeover of the US House and Senate after the midterms and the position of Hakeem Jeffries, who will become Speaker. They argue that Democratic unity is fragile, since progressives want bolder action on healthcare, immigration and foreign affairs while moderates from swing districts fear partisan fights could alienate voters focused on the economy, war and prices. They read the results as largely punitive, a rejection of the incumbent president rather than a clear ideological shift, so the party has no blank cheque. They stress structural limits: a 56-seat Senate majority falls short of the 60 votes needed to end filibusters on most legislation, and any presidential veto would need a two-thirds override. The piece concludes that the new majority must balance oversight of Trump with offering a credible legislative agenda on the economy, healthcare and energy.
brief.argument: Democrats' midterm gains give them real oversight power but not unlimited authority, and their internal divisions and Senate rules constrain what they can deliver.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Anthropic's record-breaking IPO, which raised $107bn and briefly valued the firm above $2trn, gives it a large cash cushion, but will not end its need for capital. They note the company has committed around $900bn to computing power through 2045, with about half due by 2030, a bet that depends on revenue growth. Revenue has grown much faster than the 20% annual rate that analysts at William Blair say would cover those commitments. Profitability is uneven: a brief operating profit in one quarter was followed by a loss. The company has also said its access to computing power depends on capital raised on favourable terms, and has used off-balance-sheet deals to fund chip purchases. The piece concludes that new investors may be asked to fund the company again.
brief.argument: Anthropic's huge IPO is a strong cushion, but its massive compute commitments mean it will likely need to return to capital markets.

At its heart lies a philosophical and cultural crisis, rooted in humanity’s understanding of itself and the natural world, and in the meanings we attach to freedom, progress, beauty, wealth, happiness, knowledge, and civilisation. What kind of…

brief.summary: The authors argue that the environmental crisis is at root a philosophical and cultural crisis, not only a matter of population, resource management or technology. They trace how core concepts (freedom, progress, happiness, wealth, knowledge, identity) have shifted toward control, expansion, possession and consumption, leaving nature treated as a stock of resources. Drawing on Jonas, Benjamin, Fromm, Epicurus, Heidegger, Levinas, Buber, Ubuntu, Næss and Leopold, they propose a culture of sufficiency, intellectual humility, recognition of the Other, and intergenerational responsibility, with ecosystems understood as integrated living systems whose value is not only instrumental. They close by arguing that a civilisation unable to settle disputes without war cannot claim to model progress.
brief.argument: The environmental crisis is rooted in a civilisational shift in how freedom, progress, happiness and wealth are understood, and it can be addressed only by rethinking those concepts toward sufficiency and responsibility.
recommendations: Redefine progress and wellbeing by environmental health, time for relationships and creativity, rather than by consumption and output
Distinguish needs necessary for human dignity from artificial desires encouraged by consumer culture, and organise economies around sufficiency
Extend rights and legal protections to future generations' access to water, air, soil and biodiversity
Resolve conflicts through recognition of difference and non-violent means rather than domination or war

fc9894e939b18302.title: Why the Next Bioterrorists May Not Make the Same Mistakes as Aum Shinrikyo
fc9894e939b18302.summary: In conversations with law enforcement and security professionals, one view has repeatedly emerged: Aum Shinrikyo’s failed biological weapons program in the early 1990s shows that the risk of bioterrorism is overstated, despite warnings about AI-assisted bioterrorism and calls for enhanced preparedness from experts, philanthropists, and CEOs of AI companies. The Japanese doomsday cult responsible for the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack had money, facilities, scientifically educated…

brief.summary: The authors argue that the failure of Aum Shinrikyo's bioweapons program should not be read as proof that non-state groups cannot build biological weapons. They contend Aum's failure stemmed less from missing scientists than from organisational dysfunction: secrecy limited access to expertise, rigid hierarchy promoted people by rank rather than technical judgment, and internal competition pushed programmes toward deployment without validation. Drawing on interviews with former Boko Haram members, they show how AI units could give groups repeatable routes for escalating problems and learning from failures. They say current lab-uplift studies are mixed, safeguards are uneven and open-weight models are hard to control, so risk assessments should account for AI's effect on both knowledge access and organisational structure.
brief.argument: The failure of Aum Shinrikyo's bioweapons program reflects organisational dysfunction that AI could help extremist groups overcome, so it cannot be taken as proof that future bioterrorism will fail.
recommendations: Security agencies, researchers and AI companies should jointly study how terrorists use AI and update biological risk assessments accordingly.
AI developers should combine model-level protections with rapid detection of misuse, fixes for identified jailbreaks, and access restrictions across third-party services.
Open-weight developers should filter training data from the outset of pretraining and invest in tamper-resistant safeguards before deciding on weight release.
Defence in depth should pair controls on biological materials with sustained investment in incident preparedness and response.

8a0c5836d3c03c24.summary: Europe in the Middle and in the Grey Zone bbert@hudson.org Thu, 11/19/2026 - 16:43 SVG Commentary Nov 18, 2026 International Centre for Defence and Security Europe in the Middle and in the Grey Zone Peter Rough Senior Fellow and Director, Center on Europe and Eurasia Peter Rough Commentary Caption A Eurofighter taxis to the runway at the air base in Nörvenich on December 4, 2025, as the German Air Force transfers aircraft from Tactical Air Wing 31 to the NATO border in…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute commentary by Peter Rough examines Europe's position in the middle and grey zone of security competition.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russia's hybrid campaign against Europe is cheap for Moscow and expensive for NATO, so defence alone will not suffice. They urge horizontal, asymmetric responses, including economic pressure and support for Ukrainian operations, backed by Alliance cohesion. They see Europe in a 'middle zone' of partial readiness, with NATO better suited than the EU as the vehicle for multinational deterrence, and they describe a shift from an east-west to a north-south European mosaic. On Ukraine, they say Russia's battlefield losses and economic strain contrast with its hardening negotiating demands, and they warn that US pressure on Kyiv could embolden Moscow. They judge the Black Sea and Moldova as less defended targets, while Russia's core focus remains Ukraine. They also stress cheap counter-drone methods drawn from Ukrainian experience and warn about winter pressure on Ukraine's energy grid.
brief.argument: Russia's grey zone campaign is cheap for Moscow and costly for NATO, so the West needs asymmetric, horizontal responses and cost-effective counters rather than defence alone.
recommendations: Adopt horizontal, non-symmetric responses to Russian grey zone actions, including economic campaigns and support for Ukrainian operations.
Route multinational deterrence and counter-drone initiatives through NATO rather than the EU.
Drive down the cost of counter-drone defence by adopting cheaper Ukrainian-style methods.
Avoid US pressure on Kyiv in negotiations, which would embolden Russia, and keep coordination with European partners.
brief.turkey: The Black Sea and Romania/Moldova focus, and the cost-effective counter-drone lessons, bear on Türkiye's Black Sea security and its own air defence choices.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis argues the EU-UK talks should focus on what the UK will help build rather than rejoining the EU.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the UK-EU debate should move away from the question of rejoining the EU, since the Union is itself changing through Ukraine's integration, new defence financing and new formats of association. They contend that securing Ukraine makes Britain central to this work, with France, Germany and the UK as the core, and that money and procedural disputes in the EU-UK talks should not hold back a separate strategic track. They recommend a standing consultation mechanism on the Ukraine settlement and European architecture, a modular menu of association defined before any labels, and agreed SAFE participation criteria before numbers are negotiated.
brief.argument: The UK should help co-create the next form of Europe, including new associations and Ukraine's anchoring, rather than focus on rejoining the EU.
recommendations: Give the strategic track its own standing consultation mechanism, separate from the EU-UK negotiations.
Define a modular menu of association formats before attaching labels to partner arrangements.
Agree SAFE participation criteria and principles before settling the numbers.

80a8fea69ae4bdf3.title: Beyond the Menu – Pragmatism over Purity in UK–EU Relations
80a8fea69ae4bdf3.summary: At the UK–EU Summit on 20 November, both sides should drop Brexit-era red lines and fixed institutional models in favour of pragmatic cooperation built on shared interests.

ai.sum: RUSI argues UK and EU should drop Brexit-era red lines before their 20 November summit.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the UK and EU should abandon Brexit-era red lines and fixed institutional menus (customs union, single market, full membership) in favour of pragmatic cooperation built on shared interests. They contend the old one-size-fits-all approach suited a benign security environment underpinned by US guarantees, but is ill-suited to a more volatile period as the US reduces its transatlantic security role. They recommend focusing on substance such as growth, energy prices, critical infrastructure, supply chains and defence production, rather than institutional structure. They cite the SPS deal as a model, estimating it could cut export costs by up to 8%. They also argue that the UK should not be forced into full alignment, since mutual recognition and selective divergence (for example in financial technology sandboxes) can serve both sides, as differentiation already exists within the EU through Schengen and the Eurozone. The authors note that the 2017 Brexit red lines limited negotiating room, and that difficult institutional questions need not be settled on day one.
brief.argument: The UK and EU should pursue pragmatic, substance-led cooperation, using mutual recognition and selective divergence rather than fixed institutional models and Brexit-era red lines.
recommendations: Define common interests and desired outcomes before debating institutional arrangements
Set aside early red lines to preserve negotiating leverage
Use mutual recognition and selective regulatory divergence where mutually beneficial
Defer the hardest institutional questions such as the degree of alignment

89d1e4a986732dbe.title: Europe Could Be Walking Into a Trap Over Ukraine Talks
89d1e4a986732dbe.summary: It makes sense for European leaders to have a seat at the negotiating table. But tying talks to questions of broader European security creates its own risks.

brief.summary: The author argues that European leaders are right to seek a seat at the Ukraine negotiating table, since Ukraine's future and Europe's security are increasingly intertwined. But the piece warns that the US has accepted Russia's framing that talks must cover broader European security, which could pressure Europeans into a diminished security position while Washington seeks a quick ceasefire to claim a peacemaking legacy. The author reads Russia's stated demands (rolling back NATO infrastructure to 1997 levels, halting military aid to Ukraine, blocking French and British nuclear guarantees) as maximalist and aimed at buying time to break Ukrainian resistance. To avoid the trap, Europeans should coordinate with Washington, showing why these demands harm US interests, and build on the January 2022 Western response, including reciprocal arms control and transparency proposals, before judging whether Putin is serious.
brief.argument: Europe should join the Ukraine talks but avoid being cornered into accepting a diminished European security order that Russia's maximalist demands would impose.
recommendations: Coordinate closely with the US to explain why Russian European-security demands conflict with US interests
Use the January 2022 Western response as the basis for any European security proposal, including reciprocal arms control and military transparency
Wait for Russia's answer to test whether Putin is serious before making further concessions

brief.summary: Michael Froman, CFR's president, reflects on a week-long fact-finding trip to Kenya and Ethiopia. He describes the conditions at Kakuma refugee camp, where food rations have been cut and the 2025 U.S. aid cuts have created backlogs and overcrowding, alongside examples of resilience and local enterprise. The authors argue that the aid cuts caused real humanitarian harm, though many of the underlying debates about dependency and effectiveness predate them. They contend that lasting progress depends on private-sector growth, and point to tools such as the DFC, Export-Import Bank and political risk insurance, as well as agriculture as a source of jobs. Better linkage between humanitarian and development strategy is presented as essential, with Kenya's Shirika Plan cited as an early step.
brief.argument: Humanitarian crises caused by aid cuts must be turned into an opening to reform U.S. development policy, linking humanitarian relief to private-sector-driven growth.
recommendations: Fix the government accounting rules that make it cumbersome for the DFC to provide equity financing
Use DFC, Export-Import Bank, MCC and political risk insurance tools to crowd in private investment
Better link humanitarian and development strategies, programs and resources
Support models such as Kentegra that create jobs at scale, including agricultural enterprises

0adbc5efdcc4c35f.title: Emerging Market Stablecoin Growth Is Creating Risks to Global Financial Stability
0adbc5efdcc4c35f.summary: The soaring use of U.S. dollar stablecoins with weak asset backing is a potential source of global financial instability. The IMF should act to address the problem.

brief.summary: The authors argue that dollar stablecoins with weakly backed reserves, chiefly Tether's USDT, are growing fastest in emerging markets, where they are used for converting into local currency, while the better-regulated USDC dominates in advanced economies. Using a hypothetical $6.4 billion theft from Tether, they show how a loss could erase its cushion, trigger redemption panic, and force sales of Treasury reserves into a fragile market, prompting Fed intervention. They contend that emerging-market stablecoin rules matching the US GENIUS Act and EU MiCA are needed, and that the IMF should push adoption of model legislation, including as a condition for lending. The piece is a US-focused financial stability argument, with no direct Türkiye content.
brief.argument: Weakly backed USDT's rapid growth in emerging markets could, through a reserve-draining shock, destabilise US funding markets and global financial stability unless emerging markets adopt stablecoin rules matching US and EU standards.
recommendations: Emerging markets should pass stablecoin legislation requiring reserves to be backed by safe, liquid assets, on par with the US GENIUS Act and EU MiCA.
The IMF should provide model stablecoin legislation that can be easily transposed into domestic law.
Adoption of such legislation should be a condition for IMF borrowing in high-usage countries.

brief.summary: The author argues that the ICJ's Myanmar judgment is a legal watershed: for the first time a state has been found responsible for actually committing genocide against the Rohingya. He sets out the Court's findings on killings, sexual violence, village destruction and birth-prevention measures, and the orders on prevention, investigation, punishment and reparation. He then examines contested points that will shape cases such as South Africa v. Israel: inference of genocidal intent, a duty to prevent genocide even before it occurs, and collective state intent, with the dissenters' objections noted. The piece also assesses limited enforcement prospects at the Security Council given great-power vetoes, and calls for ASEAN and Washington to press Myanmar on restitution.
brief.argument: The ICJ's Myanmar ruling breaks new legal ground on state responsibility for genocide, and its novel reasoning on intent and prevention will shape future genocide cases.
recommendations: Myanmar should plan and implement restitution for the Rohingya, including return, property, and rehabilitation.
ASEAN should press Myanmar, a member state, to comply with the Court's orders.
The United States should call on Myanmar's military regime to plan restitution and offer technical assistance.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic Congress elected in the 2026 midterms cannot deliver on affordability without confronting three linked threats. Rising fuel prices are tied to wars in Europe and the Middle East that have overextended the United States and opened room for China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. Higher electricity and water bills stem from data centres powering AI, which they say is nearing a point where machines outpace human control. Higher prices and borrowing costs reflect a national debt above $40 trillion that raises interest payments and leads foreign governments to question the dollar and Treasuries. They expect Republican leaders to confront rather than cooperate, so they urge Democrats to legislate where bipartisan openings exist and to use hearings and investigative powers elsewhere to build a case for change.
brief.argument: Democrats cannot solve the affordability crisis without addressing three interlinked threats: overextended wars, unregulated AI and an unsustainable national debt.

The piece contends Putin's main path to victory is to erode Western support for Kyiv, especially American, by exploiting President Trump's instinct to defer to him. brief.argument: Putin is using a psychological operation aimed at Trump to win in Ukraine by securing American concessions that weaken Kyiv and expose NATO's eastern members.

The post Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro outlines his vision for US leadership in the world appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro outlined his vision for US global leadership at an Atlantic Council NATO conference.

brief.summary: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, speaking at the Atlantic Council's NATO in America conference, argues that after the 2026 midterms the US has a chance to build a new foreign policy that ties security to economic prosperity. He contends that the US forgot how inseparable its economy and security are, and that allied economic strength should sit alongside mutual defence as a core purpose of alliances. He proposes an allied investment platform that speeds up permitting and investment screening, along with tax incentives and preferential financing for allied projects. He also calls for coordinated international AI regulation, including third-party oversight of frontier models, to push China toward the same rules. He criticises Trump's tariffs and his handling of the Shenzhen meeting with Xi and Putin, and urges a firm NATO commitment and continued force posture in Europe. He lists early congressional priorities such as ending the Iran war, resuming aid to Ukraine, and sanctioning Russia.
brief.argument: The authors' central claim is that the US should fuse alliance security with shared economic strength, using allied investment and coordinated AI rules, instead of the tariff-driven approach the speaker attributes to Trump.
recommendations: Create an allied investment platform that fast-tracks permitting and investment screening for transatlantic industrial projects
Offer tax incentives and preferential financing for projects from allied countries
Build international consensus on AI regulation, including third-party oversight of frontier models

brief.summary: The piece is a book roundup from Al Majalla covering two Arabic-language titles. The first, by Palestinian historian Nazmi Jubeh, is an encyclopaedic study of Jerusalem under Mamluk rule, which the authors describe as a turning point. It argues that sultans, emirs, scholars, merchants and women shaped the city through religious patronage, endowments and construction, and that Jerusalem's architecture kept the broader Mamluk style while adding local features. Jubeh documents over 100 buildings and frames heritage protection as defending history and identity. The second title, by Hamid Dabashi (translated into Arabic), argues that the Gaza genocide has shaken Western claims to defend human rights. Dabashi questions whether the problem is double standards or lies in the foundations of Western civilisation, locating it in a long history of colonialism, imperialism and racial supremacy rather than in any single government.
brief.argument: Jerusalem's Mamluk-era architecture and institutions record the city's political and religious history, while Dabashi contends that the Gaza genocide reveals deeper flaws in Western civilisation's moral claims.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 20 November EU-UK summit in Brussels, Andy Burnham's first with von der Leyen and Costa, followed the familiar pattern of European summits: deals were small and largely built on the May 2025 understanding under Starmer. The three agreements, on food and agriculture, carbon-emission trading alignment and a youth-experience scheme, are estimated by a Treasury assessment to add up to 0.5% to GDP, a fraction of Brexit's cost of 4% or more. Many implementation details remain unsettled, including UK influence over food standards, student tuition fees and access to the EU's "Made in Europe" rules. The piece shows the two sides linking the deals in bargaining, with each threatening that one could lapse if the other is not satisfied. It contrasts these minor details with Burnham's wider conversation on future relations, which is complicated by divisions within Labour and a domestic push against reversing Brexit. The authors judge that the reset may stall at electricity-market linkage, since the EU rejects cherry-picking its single market.
brief.argument: The EU-UK summit's deals are modest, unfinished and tied to bargaining, and the reset is unlikely to go far beyond electricity-market linkage because the EU refuses partial access to its single market.

brief.summary: The authors, through James M. Lindsay's essay, argue that General William Westmoreland's November 1967 National Press Club speech, given at President Johnson's request, gave an overly optimistic picture of the Vietnam War. They trace how the Americanization of the war failed to break the battlefield deadlock, how rising casualties and a shift in public opinion pressured Johnson, and how the administration chose to shore up support through favourable messaging rather than a clear change of course. The piece presents the Tet Offensive of January 1968 as exposing that rosy picture, contributing to Johnson's decision not to seek reelection. The lesson drawn is that shielding the public from unpleasant realities about overseas military operations can backfire on a president.
brief.argument: Westmoreland's overly upbeat 1967 public assessment of the Vietnam War, made to shore up political support, was discredited by the Tet Offensive and helped undermine Johnson's presidency.

ai.sum: Trump, Xi and Putin held a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, drawing comparisons to Yalta.

brief.summary: The authors read the Shenzhen summit of Trump, Xi and Putin as a Yalta-style meeting held while wars in Iran and Ukraine were still active. Its declaration did not settle either war, but two of its four provisions bear on the Middle East without naming it: stable energy flows and nuclear non-proliferation. The authors argue that energy language looks economic but carries security stakes, because Iran can threaten Hormuz and its Houthi proxies can threaten Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea without fully closing either waterway; insurance costs and rerouted shipping are enough to damage the global economy. They note the three powers share an interest in stable supply but calculate differently: China depends heavily on Gulf crude, while the US remains exposed to global price rises despite its domestic output. The piece presents the summit as a sign of great-power bargaining over the region rather than a settlement.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen declaration's energy and nuclear provisions are security measures aimed at the Iran war and Red Sea shipping, even though they are framed in economic terms.

ai.sum: Xi hosted Trump and Putin at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen in a trilateral summit that commentators say makes the world more dangerous.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen summit between Xi, Trump and Putin, despite its warm staging, masked deep divisions over Ukraine, Iran and the emerging world order. They contend the three powers share a disdain for institutions that constrain them, such as the ICC, while keeping selective multilateralism for institutions that serve them, like the Security Council veto. On arms control, they read Xi's call to ban and destroy all nuclear weapons as a polite rejection of Trump's trilateral deal rather than a real concession. China's arsenal of roughly 600 warheads is far smaller than the US and Russian stockpiles, so proportional cuts would hit Beijing first and it would not accept them. Offering total disarmament costs China nothing and casts it as the principled party.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit's displays of cordiality concealed shared contempt for binding international institutions and a Chinese refusal to disarm in step with the US and Russia.
